planting.note: Divide established clumps immediately after flowering or in early spring just as new growth begins, ensuring each division keeps several healthy roots and a growing point. 'Wakakusa' is a fully double, clear pink Japanese selection and, like other double hepaticas, does not come true from seed, so it must be propagated only by division to preserve the doubled form.

directions: Plant 'Wakakusa' in deep to dappled shade in fertile, humus-rich, reliably moist but well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil amended with leaf mold. This Japanese selection produces fully double, clear pink flowers in which the extra petals replace the fertile stamens; because the flowers are effectively sterile, they persist far longer than the single, fertile forms of the species. Handle the fleshy roots gently when dividing and do not disturb established plants otherwise, as hepaticas resent root disturbance. Best grown as a specimen pot plant or in a sheltered woodland/rock garden setting with good winter drainage.

planting.note: Divide established clumps carefully in early spring or fall, keeping each division's fleshy roots intact, and replant immediately into a cool, well-drained, humus-rich woodland bed or alpine pot with good leaf-mold content. 'Cremar' is grown chiefly for its ruffled, heavily silver-marbled foliage with a distinctive crenate (scalloped) margin, so site it where the leaves can be appreciated at close range.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in light to full shade beneath deciduous trees. 'Cremar' is a selection prized above all for its ruffled, heavily marbled leaves with a striking crenate margin; the pale to light pink flowers that appear in February and March are almost a secondary attraction compared with the foliage, which remains ornamental through the growing season. Give it decent drainage and light shade, and avoid disturbing established clumps.

planting.note: Transplant divisions with intact rhizomes in early fall, in moist, well-drained, neutral to alkaline, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees. 'Ashwood Marbles' is an English selection of the North American species, chosen for exceptionally silver-marbled, almost evergreen leaves; give it a sheltered spot with early spring sun but heavy shade after flowering and through summer.

directions: Plant in a sheltered site with moist, well-drained, alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; American hepaticas need exposure to early spring sunshine but must be well shaded immediately after flowering and through the heat of summer. 'Ashwood Marbles' bears masses of dainty pale lavender-blue flowers, occasionally tinged pink, from February to March, but its chief distinction is superb silver-marbled, nearly evergreen foliage that persists as an ornamental feature well beyond the bloom period. Very slow-growing and long-lived once established; avoid disturbing mature plants.

scientific_name: Hepatica nobilis var. pyrenaica x nobilis var. japonica 'Ashwood Charm'

planting.note: 'Ashwood Charm' is a hybrid between Hepatica nobilis var. pyrenaica and H. nobilis var. japonica and is propagated only by division. Divide established clumps in early spring, retaining intact fleshy roots per division, and pot or replant immediately into gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained compost; this hybrid is best grown under alpine-house protection rather than in the open garden.

directions: Grow 'Ashwood Charm' in a gritty, well-drained, humus-rich compost under alpine-house or cold-frame protection, or in a sheltered rock garden position in mild climates; it is classed as tender and performs best with protection from winter wet. This hybrid between the Pyrenean H. nobilis var. pyrenaica and the Japanese H. nobilis var. japonica bears beautiful pale pink bicolor flowers with contrasting red anthers over excellent, strongly marbled evergreen foliage, and flowers freely in February and March. Propagate only by division, as it will not come true from seed.
